title: Children of the Day
subtitle: 1 & 2 Thessalonians in Poems & Pictures
author: Timothy Holt
beforeYouBegin:
Paul's letters to the Thessalonians were written to a young church in a busy Macedonian port, only months after it began. They hold a household shrine left empty, a mother holding a child, a tentmaker working by lamplight so no one has to feed him, a friend sent back over the road with news, a grave visited with hope, and a lamp kept burning through the night.

This book walks through them in thirty-six short poems, in five parts: three for the first letter and two for the second. Each poem sits beside a picture and under a single line of Scripture. The pictures stay with the things the letters touch—a lamp, a loom, a loaf of bread, a road at dawn—and leave the faces to your imagination.

The poems are not the Bible. They are one reader's response to it. Open the letters to the Thessalonians alongside this book, and let the real words have the last word.

parts.title: Turned from Idols
parts.epigraph: you turned to God from idols, to serve a living and true God
parts.lightHint: Near 'three things remembered' (1 Thessalonians 1:2–3) in Part 1: Turned from Idols

parts.title: Our Glory and Our Joy
parts.epigraph: For you are our glory and our joy.
parts.lightName: Light of Our Glory and Our Joy
parts.lightHint: Near 'night and day' (1 Thessalonians 2:9) in Part 2: Our Glory and Our Joy

paintings.title: three things remembered
paintings.epigraph: “your work of faith and labor of love and perseverance of hope”
paintings.poem:
Paul didn't remember
their doctrine first.

he remembered
what their faith did with its hands,
what their love
was tired from,
what their hope
kept standing up under.

faith that works.
love that labors.
hope that holds on.

he prayed it back to God
like a list of small gifts.

someone may be praying yours
right now.
paintings.reflectionPrompt: Notice how “three things remembered” (1 Thessalonians 1:2–3) arrives at: “someone may be praying yours right now.” Who in your life is walking a hard stretch of road today and needs you to share this grace with them?

paintings.title: not in word only
paintings.epigraph: “our Good News came to you not in word only, but also in power”
paintings.poem:
words came first.
they always do.

but something else
came through the door with them,

the way warmth
comes in with bread,

the way a room changes
when the one you've waited for
steps inside.
paintings.reflectionPrompt: What if the most important thing you remember before tonight is the quiet lesson of 1 Thessalonians 1:5: “but something else came through the door with them, the way warmth comes in with bread, the way a room changes when the one you've waited for steps inside”?

paintings.title: affliction, with joy
paintings.epigraph: “having received the word in much affliction, with joy of the Holy Spirit”
paintings.poem:
they didn't wait
for a better season
to believe.

the pressure came
the same week
as the good news.

and still
there was joy,
not instead of the trouble
but right there inside it,

a flower
in the crack of the wall
that was supposed to keep it out.
paintings.reflectionPrompt: Imagine standing inside this frame beside the stones of the wall: what hurry or noise in your week begins to fade when you hear, “and still there was joy, not instead of the trouble but right there inside it, a flower in the crack of the wall that was supposed to keep it out”?

paintings.title: it went out from you
paintings.epigraph: “from you the word of the Lord has been declared”
paintings.poem:
nobody planned a campaign.

a sailor told a trader.
a trader told his wife
in another town.

the roads out of the city
carried olive oil and wool
and something new.

wherever Paul went next,
people had already heard.

a changed life
doesn't need
a messenger.
paintings.reflectionPrompt: Read the closing words aloud in the stillness: “a changed life doesn't need a messenger.” What part of your heart feels most searched or comforted by 1 Thessalonians 1:8 right now?

paintings.title: turned
paintings.epigraph: “you turned to God from idols, to serve a living and true God”
paintings.poem:
the little god in the wall niche
never heard a thing.
never needed anything
but dusting.

they turned
from what they had carried
to the One
who carries them.

from things
that stay where you set them

to a God
who is alive,
and true,
and moves toward you.
paintings.reflectionPrompt: In 1 Thessalonians 1:9, grace meets us right beside the stones of the wall: how does the closing thought—“from things that stay where you set them to a God who is alive, and true, and moves toward you”—steady your footing for the road ahead?

paintings.title: and to wait
paintings.epigraph: “to wait for his Son from heaven, whom he raised from the dead”
paintings.poem:
turning was the first half.

the second half
is waiting.

not the waiting
of a bus stop.

the waiting
of someone who has heard footsteps
on the road

and knows
whose they are.
paintings.reflectionPrompt: If today’s painting of “and to wait” (1 Thessalonians 1:10) hung beside the door you walk out of this morning, how would its final line—“the waiting of someone who has heard footsteps on the road and knows whose they are”—shape your choices?

paintings.title: bold, after Philippi
paintings.epigraph: “we grew bold in our God to tell you the Good News of God in much conflict”
paintings.poem:
they came in
with the bruises
from the last town
still on them.

any sensible man
would have kept quiet
for a while.

but boldness
wasn't something
they had.

it was something
they grew,
in God,

the way a bruise heals
from the inside.
paintings.reflectionPrompt: Every stop on the Pilgrim Walk shows how God meets us in ordinary places (1 Thessalonians 2:2)—where in your own home or work today does “it was something they grew, in God, the way a bruise heals from the inside” ring true?

paintings.title: like a nursing mother
paintings.epigraph: “But we were gentle among you, like a nursing mother cherishes her own children.”
paintings.poem:
he could have come in
with his title.

instead
he picked the gentlest picture
he knew:

a mother at night,
holding what she loves
close to the warmth,

not asking
what it will give her back.

this is what
the good news
looked like
in Thessalonica.
paintings.reflectionPrompt: Take a slow breath and read the final line again: “this is what the good news looked like in Thessalonica.” How would you walk through the next hour differently if you carried that truth with you?

paintings.title: our own souls
paintings.epigraph: “not the Good News of God only, but also our own souls”
paintings.poem:
you can hand someone a message
and keep your distance.

Paul didn't.

he gave the news
and then he gave
himself along with it,

the way you don't just
tell a hungry friend
where the bread is.

you sit down
and break yours.
paintings.reflectionPrompt: Think of a season when you knew the feeling of “you can hand someone a message and keep your distance.” Looking through the lens of 1 Thessalonians 2:8, what does it mean to discover that “you sit down and break yours”?

paintings.title: night and day
paintings.epigraph: “working night and day, that we might not burden any of you”
paintings.poem:
by day, the needle
and the heavy cloth.

by lamplight, more needle.
more cloth.

and the good news,
perhaps to whoever
stopped by to talk.

he wanted no one
to wonder
what he was after.

so he paid
for his own bread,

and gave
the best thing he had
for free.
paintings.reflectionPrompt: Look closely at the daily loaf broken in the hand in this painting (1 Thessalonians 2:9)—if you could leave one anxious weight beside it today, what would you set down?

paintings.title: as a father
paintings.epigraph: “as a father does his own children”
paintings.poem:
first a mother.
now a father.

Paul needed both
to say it:

tender enough to hold,
steady enough
to say walk this way.

encouraging.
comforting.
urging.

a hand around your hand
on the path,
until one day
you know the way yourself.
paintings.reflectionPrompt: Let your eyes rest on the brushwork and light around your own two hands: what quiet prayer rises in you when you read, “a hand around your hand on the path, until one day you know the way yourself”?

paintings.title: you are our joy
paintings.epigraph: “For you are our glory and our joy.”
paintings.poem:
the athletes of his day
ran for a crown
of leaves.

Paul looked at a room
of workers and neighbors
and former idol-keepers

and said,
there it is.

that's my crown.
paintings.reflectionPrompt: Linger with the movement in “you are our joy” (1 Thessalonians 2:19–20) from “the athletes of his day ran for a crown of leaves” to “Paul looked at a room of workers and neighbors and former idol-keepers and said, there it is. that's my crown”—where do you find yourself along that arc today?

paintings.title: alone at Athens
paintings.epigraph: “we thought it good to be left behind at Athens alone”
paintings.poem:
he could have kept Timothy.
a friend at his side
in a strange city.

instead he sent him back
up the road,
to the people
he couldn't reach.

love sometimes looks like
choosing
to be the lonely one

so someone else
can be held.
paintings.reflectionPrompt: Notice how “alone at Athens” (1 Thessalonians 3:1–2) arrives at: “love sometimes looks like choosing to be the lonely one so someone else can be held.” Who in your life is walking a hard stretch of road today and needs you to share this grace with them?

paintings.title: now we live
paintings.epigraph: “For now we live, if you stand fast in the Lord.”
paintings.poem:
all those weeks
Paul didn't know.

had the trouble
worn them down?
had they let go?

then Timothy,
dusty from the road,
with good news:

they're standing.
they miss you.

and the tired old apostle
said the most honest thing:

now we live.
paintings.reflectionPrompt: What if the most important thing you remember before tonight is the quiet lesson of 1 Thessalonians 3:6–8: “and the tired old apostle said the most honest thing: now we live”?

paintings.title: abound
paintings.epigraph: “May the Lord make you to increase and abound in love toward one another”
paintings.poem:
he didn't pray
that their love
would be enough.

he prayed it would
run over.

a cup filled
past the rim,

spilling toward each other,
and then out the door,

toward all.
paintings.reflectionPrompt: Imagine standing inside this frame beside the open threshold: what hurry or noise in your week begins to fade when you hear, “a cup filled past the rim, spilling toward each other, and then out the door, toward all”?

paintings.title: with your own hands
paintings.epigraph: “that you make it your ambition to lead a quiet life, and to do your own business, and to work with your own hands”
paintings.poem:
not the loudest life.
not the biggest.

a quiet one.

your own business,
done well.
your own hands,
tired in a good way.

ambition, Paul says,
but aimed low
and close:

a loom,
a table,
a neighbor who never wonders
if you're honest.

holiness
can look like this.
paintings.reflectionPrompt: Read the closing words aloud in the stillness: “holiness can look like this.” What part of your heart feels most searched or comforted by 1 Thessalonians 4:11–12 right now?

paintings.title: not like the rest
paintings.epigraph: “so that you don’t grieve like the rest, who have no hope”
paintings.poem:
Paul doesn't say
don't grieve.

he knows better.
tears are allowed.

he says
don't grieve
like there's no morning.

cry
with the door
left open.
paintings.reflectionPrompt: In 1 Thessalonians 4:13, grace meets us right beside the open threshold: how does the closing thought—“cry with the door left open”—steady your footing for the road ahead?

paintings.title: fallen asleep
paintings.epigraph: “God will bring with him those who have fallen asleep in Jesus”
paintings.poem:
the church had a word
for the ones they'd lost.

not gone.
not ended.

asleep.

the word you use
for someone
you expect to see
at breakfast.
paintings.reflectionPrompt: If today’s painting of “fallen asleep” (1 Thessalonians 4:14) hung beside the door you walk out of this morning, how would its final line—“the word you use for someone you expect to see at breakfast”—shape your choices?

paintings.title: forever
paintings.epigraph: “So we will be with the Lord forever.”
paintings.poem:
a shout.
a trumpet.
the ones asleep first,

then everyone else,
gathered up
together.

we don't know
how.
Paul didn't pretend to.

he just told them
where the story ends:

with the Lord.
with each other.

not for a visit.

forever.
paintings.reflectionPrompt: Every stop on the Pilgrim Walk shows how God meets us in ordinary places (1 Thessalonians 4:16–17)—where in your own home or work today does “with each other. not for a visit. forever” ring true?

paintings.title: comfort one another
paintings.epigraph: “Therefore comfort one another with these words.”
paintings.poem:
he didn't write this
to win an argument
about the end of time.

he wrote it
so someone could say it
at a graveside.

read it out loud.
hold a hand.

that's what
it's for.
paintings.reflectionPrompt: Take a slow breath and read the final line again: “hold a hand. that's what it's for.” How would you walk through the next hour differently if you carried that truth with you?

paintings.title: a thief in the night
paintings.epigraph: “But you, brothers, aren’t in darkness, that the day should overtake you like a thief.”
paintings.poem:
a thief comes
to people who are asleep
with the lights out.

but you,
Paul says,
are children of the day.

the dark
isn't your address.

leave the lamp on.
you're expecting
someone you love.
paintings.reflectionPrompt: Think of a season when you knew the feeling of “a thief comes to people who are asleep with the lights out.” Looking through the lens of 1 Thessalonians 5:4–5, what does it mean to discover that “you're expecting someone you love”?

paintings.title: breastplate and helmet
paintings.epigraph: “putting on the breastplate of faith and love, and for a helmet, the hope of salvation”
paintings.poem:
a soldier's gear
for people
who weren't soldiers.

faith and love
over the heart.

hope
around the head,

where the worry
likes to start.

stay awake.
stay dressed.

not for a battle.

for the morning.
paintings.reflectionPrompt: Look closely at the quiet centerpiece of “breastplate and helmet” in this painting (1 Thessalonians 5:8)—if you could leave one anxious weight beside it today, what would you set down?

paintings.title: always, without ceasing, in everything
paintings.epigraph: “Always rejoice. Pray without ceasing. In everything give thanks”
paintings.poem:
three short lines.
the shortest verses
in the letter.

rejoice.
pray.
give thanks.

not a schedule.
a flame you keep lit
while you do everything else.

kneading.
mending.
walking to the well.
paintings.reflectionPrompt: Let your eyes rest on the brushwork and light around the stone well in the heat of the day: what quiet prayer rises in you when you read, “mending. walking to the well”?

paintings.title: faithful
paintings.epigraph: “He who calls you is faithful, who will also do it.”
paintings.poem:
spirit, soul and body,
the whole of you,
kept whole.

it sounds like
too much to ask.

it is.

that's why
the last line
isn't about you.

the One who called
is faithful.

he'll finish
what he started.
paintings.reflectionPrompt: Linger with the movement in “faithful” (1 Thessalonians 5:23–24) from “spirit, soul and body, the whole of you, kept whole” to “he'll finish what he started”—where do you find yourself along that arc today?

paintings.title: growing
paintings.epigraph: “your faith grows exceedingly, and the love of each and every one of you toward one another abounds”
paintings.poem:
the trouble
didn't stop.

neither did
the growing.

when Paul writes again,
and he can't help it:

your faith
is taller.

your love,
every one of you,
is wider.

some trees
put down the deepest roots
in the rockiest ground.
paintings.reflectionPrompt: Notice how “growing” (2 Thessalonians 1:3) arrives at: “some trees put down the deepest roots in the rockiest ground.” Who in your life is walking a hard stretch of road today and needs you to share this grace with them?

paintings.title: relief
paintings.epigraph: “to give relief to you who are afflicted with us”
paintings.poem:
they were tired
of being the ones
who suffered for being good.

Paul doesn't tell them
it doesn't matter.

he tells them
God sees,
and God is fair,

and when the Lord is revealed
there will be relief,

like cool water
at the end
of a long hot road.
paintings.reflectionPrompt: What if the most important thing you remember before tonight is the quiet lesson of 2 Thessalonians 1:6–7: “he tells them God sees, and God is fair, and when the Lord is revealed there will be relief, like cool water at the end of a long hot road”?

paintings.title: glorified in you
paintings.epigraph: “that the name of our Lord Jesus may be glorified in you, and you in him”
paintings.poem:
glass doesn't
make the light.

it just
lets it through,

and somehow
it's more beautiful
for having been held.

his name in you.
you in him.

the light,
and the one
it shines through,

both shining.
paintings.reflectionPrompt: Imagine standing inside this frame beside the name by which He calls you: what hurry or noise in your week begins to fade when you hear, “the light, and the one it shines through, both shining”?

paintings.title: not quickly shaken
paintings.epigraph: “not to be quickly shaken in your mind, and not be troubled”
paintings.poem:
rumors ran through the church:
a letter,
a voice,
someone who said
it's already over,
you missed it.

Paul wrote back.

no.
don't be shaken.
remember what I told you.

every age
has its alarm bells.

he still says
the same thing:

stay steady.
he hasn't forgotten you.
paintings.reflectionPrompt: Read the closing words aloud in the stillness: “every age has its alarm bells. he hasn't forgotten you.” What part of your heart feels most searched or comforted by 2 Thessalonians 2:1–2 right now?

paintings.title: chosen from the beginning
paintings.epigraph: “God chose you from the beginning for salvation”
paintings.poem:
before the dock,
before the loom,
before the idols in the wall,

before
they had anything
to offer,

God had chosen them.

and whatever loud voices
said about the end,

Paul pointed them
back to the beginning.
paintings.reflectionPrompt: In 2 Thessalonians 2:13, grace meets us right beside the stones of the wall: how does the closing thought—“and whatever loud voices said about the end, Paul pointed them back to the beginning”—steady your footing for the road ahead?

paintings.title: good hope
paintings.epigraph: “gave us eternal comfort and good hope through grace”
paintings.poem:
not a thin hope.
not a maybe.

good hope.

the kind that
keeps you warm
the way a banked fire does
through the night,

and is still there
in the morning
when you reach for it.
paintings.reflectionPrompt: If today’s painting of “good hope” (2 Thessalonians 2:16–17) hung beside the door you walk out of this morning, how would its final line—“the kind that keeps you warm the way a banked fire does through the night, and is still there in the morning when you reach for it”—shape your choices?

paintings.title: that the word may run
paintings.epigraph: “pray for us, that the word of the Lord may spread rapidly”
paintings.poem:
the great apostle
asks the small church
to pray for him.

not for comfort.
for the word
to run.

the way news runs
down a road
ahead of the runner.
paintings.reflectionPrompt: Every stop on the Pilgrim Walk shows how God meets us in ordinary places (2 Thessalonians 3:1)—where in your own home or work today does “the way news runs down a road ahead of the runner” ring true?

paintings.title: the Lord is faithful
paintings.epigraph: “But the Lord is faithful, who will establish you and guard you from the evil one.”
paintings.poem:
not all have faith,
Paul says.

and then,
almost in the same breath:

but the Lord
is faithful.

the world
can be unreliable.

he isn't.
paintings.reflectionPrompt: Take a slow breath and read the final line again: “the world can be unreliable. he isn't.” How would you walk through the next hour differently if you carried that truth with you?

paintings.title: into God's love
paintings.epigraph: “May the Lord direct your hearts into God’s love, and into the perseverance of Christ.”
paintings.poem:
a heart
can wander off
in any direction.

so he prays
it will be steered,

like water
finding its way
downhill

into God's love,

and into the patience
of the One
who never
gave up on us.
paintings.reflectionPrompt: Think of a season when you knew the feeling of “a heart can wander off in any direction.” Looking through the lens of 2 Thessalonians 3:5, what does it mean to discover that “so he prays it will be steered, like water finding its way downhill into God's love, and into the patience of the One who never gave up on us”?

paintings.title: your own bread
paintings.epigraph: “that they work with quietness and eat their own bread”
paintings.poem:
some had stopped working.
the Lord was coming,
so why bother?

Paul's answer
was plain:

pick up your tools.
work quietly.
eat your own bread.

waiting well
looks a lot like
an ordinary workday,

done faithfully.
paintings.reflectionPrompt: Look closely at the stone well in the heat of the day in this painting (2 Thessalonians 3:10–12)—if you could leave one anxious weight beside it today, what would you set down?

paintings.title: don't grow weary
paintings.epigraph: “But you, brothers, don’t be weary in doing what is right.”
paintings.poem:
good is heavy
some days.

the same kindness,
the same work,
the same prayer,
and nothing seems to move.

don't be weary,
he says.

not because
it's easy.

because it's right.

and because
the One you're doing it for
is coming.
paintings.reflectionPrompt: Let your eyes rest on the brushwork and light around the quiet centerpiece of “don't grow weary”: what quiet prayer rises in you when you read, “and because the One you're doing it for is coming”?

paintings.title: in my own hand
paintings.epigraph: “Now may the Lord of peace himself give you peace at all times in all ways.”
paintings.poem:
at the end
he takes the pen
from the one writing for him,

and adds a line
in his own hand,

so they'll know
it's really him.

peace,
he writes.

at all times.
in all ways.

the Lord
be with you all.
paintings.reflectionPrompt: Linger with the movement in “in my own hand” (2 Thessalonians 3:16–17) from “at the end he takes the pen from the one writing for him, and adds a line in his own hand, so they'll know it's really him” to “at all times. the Lord be with you all”—where do you find yourself along that arc today?
